title: Modbus register map
description: The Modbus interface of one device, entire: which device it is, how a client recognises it, which exceptions it raises, what the transport tolerates, the address spaces it exposes, and the commissioning procedures it supports. A space owns the numbering its registers are written in and the registers themselves; a register owns its address, prose and access; a field owns one property's identity, wire encoding and meaning. There is no second document: everything a consumer needs in order to talk to the device, document it, or generate code for it is here.

device.description: Which device this register map belongs to. Required: a map is useless to a client that cannot tell what it is a map of, and a repository holding many devices across many firmware versions needs each file to say which one it is (D14). Vendor and model identify the product; everything else is optional.

vendor.description: Who makes the device. Named explicitly because this format describes third-party products too.

model.description: The product, as its datasheet names it. The same thing the semantic document calls 'name', where one exists.

description.description: One line on what the device is.

type.description: The vendor's own numeric product id, where it has one, as read from the device itself. Often the most discriminating thing identification can match on.

firmware_version.description: Which firmware versions this map is valid for. A range rather than one version, because a register map normally outlives several releases; omitting 'to' means this version and later.

identification.description: How a client decides that the device answering at some address is this device, and so that this profile applies. A bus scan finds an address, not a product: without this, choosing a profile is left to whoever is holding the laptop. Every rule given must hold, so a profile matching nothing is safer than one matching the wrong device. Where a device implements Read Device Identification (FC 43), that is the cheapest and safest first probe, and register probes narrow it further or stand in for it entirely where it is absent.

items.description: One read whose result must match for this profile to apply. Reads only: probing an unidentified device must never change it. A read that fails -- an exception, a timeout, a short frame -- is a mismatch and not an error, because the device being probed may be a different product entirely.

mask.description: Applied to the raw value before comparing, for a register that packs a product id beside something volatile -- a version byte beside a build counter, say.

equals.description: The raw register value, before any scale or enum mapping. Raw because a decode would presume the very profile being tested.

in.description: Any of these raw values matches. For a product id shared by a family of models this map covers.

range.description: An inclusive [low, high] band of raw values, for matching a firmware version range.

registers.description: Register reads that must all match, cheapest and most discriminating first. A client may stop at the first mismatch.

read_device_id.description: Expected objects from Read Device Identification -- function code 43 with MEI type 14 -- for a device that implements it. This is the only way to ask a Modbus device what it is without already knowing its register map, which makes it the right first probe wherever it is available: it cannot misread a reserved address on a stranger's device the way a register probe can. It is optional in Modbus and widely unimplemented, which is why register probes stand alongside it rather than being replaced by it. Requires 43 in limits.supported_fc. Strings are compared after trimming surrounding whitespace; a device may pad them.

vendor_name.description: Object 0x00, the only object a conformity level 1 device must return besides product code and revision.

product_code.description: Object 0x01. Usually the most discriminating of the three basic objects.

major_minor_revision.description: Object 0x02, the firmware revision as the device reports it -- free-form text, not necessarily matching device.firmware_version.

product_name.description: Object 0x04, regular identification. Absent on a conformity level 1 device.

conformity_level.description: What the device returns for MEI 14, as reported in the response: 1 basic, 2 regular, 3 extended, and 0x81-0x83 for the same levels with individual object access. Stating it tells a client which objects it may ask for, and whether it may request one by id instead of the whole stream.

exceptions.description: Which exception codes this device raises and what it means by them. Two reasons this cannot be left to the Modbus specification. A manufacturer may overload a standard code, so a client displaying the standard text out of its own table would be confidently wrong; and a manufacturer may define codes of its own, which a client can otherwise only show as a bare number. Without this section an integrator cannot tell a refused write from a broken bus, which is the difference between a configuration mistake and a site visit.

limits.description: Transport-level facts about what this device tolerates, as opposed to what Modbus permits.

supported_fc.description: Function codes this device answers. 17 is Report Server ID and 43 is Read Device Identification (with MEI type 14) -- both are identification rather than data access, both are optional in Modbus, and 43 is the one identification.read_device_id relies on, so it has to be declarable here or a profile can expect a call the device never claimed to support.

spaces.description: The address spaces this device exposes, each owning its numbering and its registers. Spaces are independent ranges -- the same number in two spaces is two different registers -- so they are containers here rather than a tag repeated on every entry. A space the device does not expose is simply absent, which is what says so.

holding.description: The holding register space: 16-bit read-write registers, reached by FC 3, 6 and 16.

base.description: The address this document would write for wire offset 0 in this space, so offset = address - base. 1 for the register numbers a datasheet prints, 0 for raw offsets, or the legacy Modicon base directly -- 40001 for holding, 30001 for input -- which lets a map be transcribed exactly as printed. Required: an off-by-one here is wrong in the documentation, the commissioning tool and the firmware at once, with no diff anywhere to show it, and nothing about it is derivable. It lives on the space because it is a fact about that space's numbering and about nothing else.

allOf.description: A register that carries something in a read-write space has to state its access. The Modbus specification characterises the holding-register table as read-write but guarantees nothing per address: it leaves the mapping onto device memory entirely to the vendor, so a read-only or write-only holding register conforms, and a client cannot discover which by probing. A default of read_write would therefore be the format asserting what the protocol does not. A reserved range is exempt: it carries nothing to have access to.

input.description: The input register space: 16-bit read-only registers, reached by FC 4. An input register is read-only by virtue of FC 4, and a discrete input by virtue of FC 2, so `access` adds nothing there and is not required.

base.description: The address this document would write for wire offset 0 in this space, so offset = address - base. 1 for the register numbers a datasheet prints, 0 for raw offsets, or the legacy Modicon base directly -- 40001 for holding, 30001 for input -- which lets a map be transcribed exactly as printed. Required: an off-by-one here is wrong in the documentation, the commissioning tool and the firmware at once, with no diff anywhere to show it, and nothing about it is derivable. It lives on the space because it is a fact about that space's numbering and about nothing else.

coil.description: The coil space: single read-write bits, reached by FC 1, 5 and 15.

base.description: The address this document would write for wire offset 0 in this space, so offset = address - base. 1 for the register numbers a datasheet prints, 0 for raw offsets, or the legacy Modicon base directly -- 40001 for holding, 30001 for input -- which lets a map be transcribed exactly as printed. Required: an off-by-one here is wrong in the documentation, the commissioning tool and the firmware at once, with no diff anywhere to show it, and nothing about it is derivable. It lives on the space because it is a fact about that space's numbering and about nothing else.

The Modbus specification characterises the holding-register table as read-write but guarantees nothing per address: it leaves the mapping onto device memory entirely to the vendor, so a read-only or write-only holding register conforms, and a client cannot discover which by probing. A default of read_write would therefore be the format asserting what the protocol does not. A reserved range is exempt: it carries nothing to have access to.

discrete.description: The discrete input space: single read-only bits, reached by FC 2. An input register is read-only by virtue of FC 4, and a discrete input by virtue of FC 2, so `access` adds nothing there and is not required.

procedures.description: Ordered sequences of reads and writes a commissioning tool runs against this device. They live here because every step is a Modbus operation; steps name fields by the identifier a field's `property` gives.

identifier.description: Also has to be a valid C identifier: the firmware X-macro pastes these into token names.

exception.description: One exception code this device raises, and what it means by it. Listing a code says the device can return it, which is worth stating on its own: it tells an integrator what to expect and a commissioning tool which failures are normal rather than a broken bus. Both texts are required on every entry, standard codes included, so a consumer never needs a table of its own in order to render one.

code.description: The exception code byte, as it arrives in the response after the function code with its high bit set. 1-6, 8, 10 and 11 are the codes Modbus defines; anything else is this vendor's own. Which of the two a code is follows from the number, so it is not declared -- validate.py holds the standard table.

name.description: Short label for inline display -- a status line, a log entry, a cell in a table of failures -- where there is no room for the description. Capped at 40 characters, which is the longest name Modbus itself uses ('Gateway Target Device Failed To Respond', 39), so a consumer can lay out a fixed column knowing nothing will overflow it. Deliberately not called 'title' as a register's short text is: a register title is a full uncapped name, and several of them would not fit inline.

description.description: What this device means by the code, and what a client should do about it. For a standard code used as intended this may elaborate on the circumstances without contradicting them; where it contradicts them, set 'overloads'.

overloads.description: Present, and always true, when this device gives a STANDARD code a meaning that departs from the standard one. Since name and description are always given, this is not about supplying text -- it is the machine-readable warning that goes with it. A client that knows the standard table can stop applying logic keyed to the standard meaning (retry policy, diagnosis, how it phrases the failure to an installer), and generated documentation can mark the code as used non-standardly. Meaningful only on a standard code: a proprietary code overloads nothing, having had no prior meaning to depart from. Never written as false; an absent key already says that.

retryable.description: Whether repeating the identical request can succeed later. True where the device is merely busy or still committing, false where the request is malformed or refused outright. Worth stating on a proprietary code, since a client has no way to guess it; on a standard code it is already implied -- 5 and 6 are retryable, 1 to 3 are not -- so stating it there documents the obvious, and contradicting the implication is an error.

address.description: An address in the numbering its space declares. The wire offset is address - base, and the legal window is therefore base .. base + 65535, which validate.py enforces -- a schema cannot see a sibling key. The bound here is merely generous enough for six-digit Modicon numbering.

field.description: One property carried by this register, whole or as a single bit -- and everything a consumer needs in order to decode, display, validate and condition it. The identifier in `property` is the property's only name: expressions and procedures reference it.

property.description: Name of the property in the properties document.

encoding.description: How the value is packed, in a 16-bit space. Required, and deliberately not derived from the property's range even though the narrowest fitting width is correct in 178 of 190 cases here: deriving it would let a range widened in the semantic document silently change the wire format, which is a protocol break with no diff in this file (D16). A width wider than one register makes this register span the following addresses too.

bit.description: Bit position, for a bool packed into this register. No encoding is given: a bit is a bit.

count.description: Element count for an array or a string. Array length, not register span.

type.description: What the value IS, as against how this register carries it. Stated rather than derived from the presence of `enum`, `labels` or `scale`: that derivation is exact on a scaled integer map and wrong the moment a device sends a genuine float32, which carries no scale (D16's reason for keeping `encoding` explicit, in the other direction).

max_length.description: Maximum character count, for type 'text' only.

labels.description: Names for a bool's two states, e.g. { false: disabled, true: enabled }. What documentation and a commissioning tool show, and what an expression may compare against.

title.description: The field's name. Required where the register carries more than one, since a lone field's name is its register's name (D18).

description.description: Prose for this field specifically. A register carrying one field keeps its prose on the register.

variants.description: Alternative interpretations of the same register, one per configuration. A single variant is a modelling mistake: use top-level presentation instead.

constraints.description: Range/default/step that depend on configuration. First matching entry wins.

reread.description: What to re-read after writing this signal. The literal 'dependents' resolves against the derived reverse index; an explicit list covers registers the device re-clamps without any expression saying so.

default.description: Factory default, in engineering units or as an enum member -- what a factory reset restores and what a commissioning tool offers as a starting value. Where the default depends on configuration, put it in `constraints` instead.

space.description: Which Modbus address space. These are independent ranges: the same number in two spaces is two different registers.

word_register.description: One register in a 16-bit space, or a reserved range of them. Its space is the block it sits in, which also fixes its numbering. A bool packed into it is a field with a `bit` position; `bit` is not an encoding here, because it would not say which bit -- that shape belongs to the single-bit spaces, and is unrepresentable in this one.

allOf.description: A clear_label only means something for a register carrying bits.
A reserved range carries nothing; anything else carries something.
A register carrying more than one property needs its own name: there is no single property to borrow one from.
A count is an element count, so it belongs to an encoding that has elements. Only 'chars' does.

title.description: The register's name in the register map. Optional when it carries exactly one property, which lends its title.

description.description: Prose for the register map. A register carrying several properties has no property to borrow this from, which is the reason registers are entities here.

access.description: Access over the bus. Absent means read_write, which is what a holding register normally is. An input register is read-only by virtue of the function code that reaches it, so stating it there says nothing. Required to be stated wherever it differs, since with the semantic document gone there is no property access left to derive it from.

reserved.description: Why this range carries nothing: reserved for future use, withdrawn, vendor-private. The prose is the point -- a bare gap is indistinguishable from an oversight.

clear_label.description: What this register means when none of its bits is set, e.g. "OK". Only for a register carrying bits. Found missing by generating a 3SModbus library profile, whose bitwise decoder requires such a label and which the format could not supply (D16); a register map document needs it for the same reason.

hidden.description: Service register: real, documented, not shown to an ordinary user. Never written as false; an absent key already says that.

bit_register.description: One coil or discrete input, or a reserved range of them. A coil IS one bit and its address selects it, so there is exactly one property, no encoding to choose, no bit position to give -- the address already was one -- and no clear_label, since there is no set of bits to be collectively clear. None of that is a rule checked here: it is the shape.

property.description: The single bool this coil carries. Named directly rather than through a `fields` list: a list of one is a list that exists only to be indexed.

title.description: The coil's name in the register map.

access.description: A discrete input is inherently read-only; a coil is normally read-write. State it only where this device offers less.

reserved.description: Why this range carries nothing. The prose is the point -- a bare gap is indistinguishable from an oversight.

hidden.description: Service register: real, documented, not shown to an ordinary user. Never written as false; an absent key already says that.

expression.description: Boolean expression over field identifiers and enum member names. The reverse-dependency index is built by collecting identifiers out of these, so the grammar must stay small and total (DECISIONS.md D1). The grammar itself is not yet pinned down -- OPEN-QUESTIONS.md Q2.

enum_member.description: Enum member name. Uppercase is allowed and often right -- acronyms like LPG read wrong lowercased, and C enum constants are conventionally uppercase. Must still be a valid C identifier for the X-macro. Member names are compared case-sensitively wherever expressions mention them.

value.description: A register value: an integer, a boolean, an enum member name, or a procedure parameter reference.

range.description: [min, max] in engineering units, after scale is applied.

enum_map.description: Raw register value -> member name. Mutually exclusive states.

presentation.description: How a raw value becomes an engineering value. Shared by a signal and by each of its variants.

decimals.description: Decimal places to show. Display only -- scale already fixes the value.

display.description: How an int is rendered. 'version' means the raw bytes shown as hex and dot-joined with the leading zero trimmed, so 0x0130 reads as 1.30 -- which is 50 of the 55 bytewise decoders in the company library. Display only: the value is an integer.

danger.description: Drives how loudly the commissioning tool asks before running.

confirm.description: Shown verbatim before running. Says what breaks, not 'are you sure'.

duration_ms.description: Expected wall time, for progress UI.

enum_from.description: Take the allowed values from that signal's enum.

property_ref.description: The identifier of a field's `property` somewhere in this map. Procedures and expressions name fields by it, which is why it survived the semantic document it was defined in: it is the one name a device property has.
